concerns.title: Tuning/evaluation mismatch and dataset construction choices
concerns.description: Parts of MORSE were tuned on MC data (which the authors argue has weaknesses), then evaluated on SD17; evaluation-control decisions may inflate perceived gains and confound claims about semantic contributions.
evidence: §4.2: 'all systems use the development dataset as a test dataset, and the training dataset is used for tuning MORSE’s hyperparameters.'
§5.2: authors used 5-fold CV for SD17 (MORSE-CV), but MORSE reported elsewhere was tuned on MC.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify which experiments used which tuning sets; prefer evaluating all models with tuning restricted to each target dataset (or use held-out tuning sets consistently). Provide results when MORSE is tuned solely on SD17 to isolate dataset effects.

concerns.title: Ad-hoc threshold for difference-vector consistency
concerns.description: The operational test for vector equality (cos(~w4, ~w2 - ~w1 + ~w3) > 0.1) is weakly motivated; such a low cosine might accept noisy relations and its absolute meaning depends on vector training.
evidence: §3.1 definition of clusterr uses cosine > 0.1 without justification or alternative thresholds.
No error bars or calibration experiments shown for the relation between cosine threshold and precision/recall.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results across a sweep of cosine thresholds (e.g., 0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) and show how scorer_sem and the final segmentation metrics respond; consider normalizing for vector norms or using cosine distributions on held-out morphology/non-morphology pairs to justify threshold selection.

concerns.title: Novelty claim needs tighter literature positioning
concerns.description: The paper claims to be the 'first' to use vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency in morpheme segmentation, but related work (e.g., Soricut & Och 2015 and others using difference vectors or corpus-level signals) are cited—differences should be explicitly delineated so the novelty claim is credible.
evidence: §2 cites Soricut & Och (2015) as inspiration and §3.1 uses difference vectors; the paper claims novelty but does not precisely state how it departs from that prior art.
Related semantic morpheme works (Narasimhan et al. 2015, Schone & Jurafsky 2000) are cited but distinctions could be clearer.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a short focused subsection that compares MORSE's vocabulary-wide clustering/statistics and inference strategy to Soricut & Och (2015) and other semantic approaches, listing conceptual and algorithmic differences and clearly qualifying any 'first' claims.

concerns.title: Limited evaluation on morphological diversity and statistical significance
concerns.description: Evaluation covers three languages but key claims about generality vs. failure modes lack statistical testing and deeper probing (e.g., rare affix recovery, per-affix precision, effect of embedding quality).
evidence: §5 shows language-level F1 numbers but no per-affix analysis, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
Finnish failure is discussed qualitatively but no controlled experiment demonstrates the degree to which vocabulary cap or embedding degradation cause the failure.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-affix or per-rule analyses, bootstrap confidence intervals on reported F1, and controlled ablations that vary corpus size/embedding hyperparameters; include experiments on simulated sparsity to isolate failure causes.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary orthography-only baseline and widely used MDL-based morpheme segmentation system.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Morfessor relies on MDL and orthographic signals; MORSE integrates semantic signals and difference-vector consistency on top of orthographic candidate enumeration.
comparable_works.source_trace: References: Creutz and Lagus (2002, 2005, 2007); paper uses Morfessor as main baseline (§2, §4, §5)

comparable_works.relevance: Published state-of-the-art semantic-aware segmentation approach referenced for comparison.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Narasimhan et al. incorporate semantic relatedness in a log-linear model for morphological chains; MORSE differs by emphasizing vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency and a greedy orthographic+semantic inference.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in Related Work and Results (§2, §5)

comparable_works.relevance: Prior use of difference vectors/distr. semantics for morphological/lexical transformations that inspired MORSE's vocabulary-wide vector treatment.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Soricut & Och applied difference-vector heuristics for morphological discovery and lexicon mapping; MORSE operationalizes a corpus-wide clustering/consistency measure and integrates it into segmentation inference.

comparable_works.relevance: Earlier works incorporating semantic similarity for morphological relation discovery.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These works rely on local semantic relatedness (LSA or mutual information) between candidate pairs; MORSE augments local checks with vocabulary-wide vector consistency.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in §1 and §2 as prior semantic attempts

uncertainty_flags: The 1M vocabulary cap's operational impact on scorer_sem and support set coverage is substantial but not fully quantified.
Thresholds (e.g., cosine > 0.1) and other hyperparameters are presented but lacking calibration and statistical justification.
Comparisons to published SOTA rely on reported numbers which may not be strictly comparable without reproduction under identical pre-processing, vocab and embedding conditions.
The SD17 dataset is targeted to compositionality but sampling from top 10k frequency words may bias towards frequent/regular morphology; generalization to lower-frequency phenomena is uncertain.
Greedy inference may produce cascading errors; no global decoding baseline is provided.
alternative_interpretations: The reported gains (especially on SD17) might partly reflect tuning or dataset construction choices (SD17 was designed for compositionality) rather than purely a novel algorithmic advantage.
MORSE's advantage on English/Turkish may be due to better coverage of high-frequency affix patterns in the 1M vocabulary rather than the vocabulary-wide semantic signal per se.

Finnish failures could indicate that the method is not robust to agglutinative morphology generally, not only a vocab-size limit; different morphological phenomena (non-concatenative or long concatenations) may require other modeling choices.
Some improvement could stem from orthographic heuristics (support set size) interacting with semantic thresholds; separate effect sizes for each component are not fully isolated.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides code and dataset links, but some provided URLs use a 'dropproxy' intermediate; durable repositories (e.g., GitHub/Zenodo) would aid reproducibility.

Important experimental details (exact hyperparameter values chosen per language, random seeds, number of Word2Vec negative samples/epochs, pre-processing scripts and vocabulary construction) are not exhaustively listed in the main text or appendix.
Comparative baselines (Morfessor variants, their hyperparameters) are not fully detailed; confirmatory reproduction would require these specifics.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The conceptual novelty of scoring rules using corpus-level difference-vector consistency is plausible and interesting, but novelty alone does not guarantee empirical robustness—validation requires sensitivity analyses, broader language coverage, and ablations isolating the vocabulary-wide signal from other cues.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If high-quality word embeddings (trained on very large corpora) accurately capture morphological regularities, then vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency will reliably validate affix rules and improve segmentation.
If vocabulary coverage is large enough that support sets SS_r contain many bona fide morphological pairs, scorer_sem will be informative; conversely, severe sparsity will undermine the method.
If hyperparameters governing vector-consistency thresholds are chosen robustly (via cross-validation or principled calibration), the framework will avoid admitting noisy difference vectors.
If inference is improved from greedy to a global/beam search, cascading segmentation errors will decrease and gains will become more stable across morphological typologies.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The explicit use of corpus-wide difference-vector consistency to validate orthographic affix rules is a new framing in morpheme segmentation that shifts attention from local pairwise checks to a global regularity signal; this conceptual move could open new lines of research connecting embedding arithmetic and morphological inference.
evidence: Paper formalizes scorer_sem and scorew_sem as corpus-level measures (§3.1).
Authors cite Soricut & Och (2015) but claim a different operationalization for segmentation.
uncertainty_flags: Need clearer differentiation from prior difference-vector work and more robust empirical ablation to establish the unique contribution of the vocabulary-wide metric.

novelty_lenses.rationale: While the vocabulary-wide difference-vector idea is interesting, the overall system still relies on orthodox orthographic enumeration and greedy inference; without stronger ablation and broader multilingual validation, the work could be seen as an effective engineering integration of known signals rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm.
evidence: Related work already combines local semantic similarity with orthography (Schone & Jurafsky, Narasimhan et al.), and Soricut & Och used difference vectors for related tasks.
Key algorithmic pieces (support set enumeration, score combination, greedy inference) are standard engineering choices.
uncertainty_flags: Distinguishing disruption vs incremental advance depends on follow-up studies that show the vocabulary-wide signal drives independent gains across typologically diverse languages and under varying data regimes.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have moderate confidence in the high-level claims (integration of vocabulary-wide semantics can help segmentation) because the paper supplies formal definitions and empirical gains on carefully constructed datasets. However, reproducibility and the generality of the claims are uncertain due to missing hyperparameter detail, the 1M vocabulary cap, limited ablation, and sensitivity of cosine thresholds—hence a mid-range confidence interval.

prior_stage_inputs: Prior stage digests from reviewers 1-4 (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive) summarizing MORSE method, experiments, strengths and concerns.
Shared analysis noting implementation/hyperparameter and vocabulary-truncation uncertainty flags.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents MORSE, an unsupervised/weakly-supervised morpheme segmentation framework that augments orthographic candidate-rule induction with two semantic validators: (1) local pairwise semantic relatedness (cosine similarity of word embeddings) and (2) a vocabulary-wide consistency check based on equality/consistency of difference vectors across many support pairs for a candidate orthographic transformation. The training stage enumerates candidate add/replace affix rules and support sets from surface-form pairs, then computes orthographic support counts, pair-level cosine scores, and rule-level and pair-level offset-consistency scores derived from comparing difference vectors. Inference greedily applies rules that meet threshold hyperparameters, iteratively segmenting words (Radd first, then Rrep). Experiments train Word2Vec (300d, window=5) on Wikipedia and compare MORSE to Morfessor on Morpho Challenge (English, Turkish, Finnish) and on a newly created semantically-driven English dataset (SD17). Reported results: MORSE improves boundary-F1 vs Morfessor on English and Turkish (absolute gains ~6–7% on MC), large gains on SD17 (~24% absolute), but underperforms on Finnish (attributed to vocabulary cap and data sparsity). Authors also show fewer false positive segmentations on a small curated non-compositional set (7 vs 43) and provide some hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning-size analysis. Key methodological gaps persist in reported experiments: underspecified embedding/training hyperparameters and seeds, asymmetric constraint (MORSE limited to top 1M vocab while Morfessor is not), lack of controlled ablation isolating vocabulary-wide offset consistency vs local cosine vs orthographic score, sparse statistical reporting (variance, significance), and limited quantification of how vocabulary truncation affects support sets and results. I mark claims as supported/partially supported/overstated in the identified_claims below using manuscript evidence.
logical_argument_graph: Orthographic-only segmentation (MDL, Morfessor) oversegments because orthographic change is necessary but not sufficient evidence of morphological/semantic compositionality (motivating example: 'freshman').
Distributional word embeddings capture morpho-syntactic regularities; difference vectors can encode affix transformations (Mikolov et al. motivation).
If many orthographically matching pairs exhibit consistent difference vectors, the orthographic transformation likely corresponds to a productive morphological process (vocabulary-wide validator).
If an orthographic candidate pair also has high local cosine similarity, it likely is semantically related (local validator).
Combine orthographic support size with the two semantic validators to filter rules/pairs and drive inference (MORSE algorithm).
Evaluate MORSE against Morfessor and prior baselines on MC and SD17; improvements on compositionality-aware data indicate semantic signals help reduce oversegmentation and improve boundary-F1.
Failure on Finnish linked to data sparsity and 1M vocabulary cap reducing availability of support pairs, showing limitation in agglutinative/rich-morphology languages.

identified_claims.claim_label: MORSE integrates vocabulary-wide and local semantics to improve segmentation
identified_claims.claim_text: MORSE, a new framework that integrates vocabulary-wide and local semantic signals (difference vectors and cosine similarities) with orthographic rules, yields better morpheme segmentation than prior unsupervised/weakly supervised methods.
evidence: Algorithm description in Sections 3.1 (scorer_sem, scorew_sem, scoreloc_sem) and 3.2 (inference using semantic + orthographic thresholds).
Table 3 shows higher F1 for MORSE than Morfessor on MC English (70.32 vs 64.35) and Turkish (38.07 vs 31.01).
SD17 results: MORSE-CV shows large gains (reported ~24% absolute over Morfessor in text).
Non-compositional set: MORSE generated 7 false morphemes vs Morfessor's 43.
uncertainty_flags: Hyperparameters used to produce reported numbers are not fully tabulated; tuning procedure differs (MORSE tuned on gold dev; unknown whether Morfessor hyperparameters were tuned equivalently).
Vocabulary cap (1M) applied only to MORSE could bias comparisons, especially across languages; scaling effects are not quantified.
No ablation isolating which semantic signal (local cosine vs offset-consistency) drives the gains—so the integrated claim is partially supported but mechanistic attribution is uncertain.

identified_claims.claim_label: Vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency is novel and helpful
identified_claims.claim_text: Considering vocabulary-wide consistency of difference vectors is novel for morpheme segmentation and helps validate affix rules beyond local pairwise semantic similarity.
evidence: Paper defines scorer_sem(r) and scorew_sem((w1,w2)) that rely on counting pair-pair offset agreements across support sets (Section 3.1).
Related Work cites Soricut & Och (2015) and positions MORSE as first to use difference-vector consistency at vocabulary-wide scale specifically for morpheme segmentation (Related Work).
uncertainty_flags: Claim of being 'first' is plausible within the presented morpheme-segmentation literature but depends on precise definitions; Soricut & Och used offsets for morphology induction—differentiation is asserted but not fully documented.
No ablation quantifies the unique contribution of vocabulary-wide offset consistency vs local cosine; thus the claimed causal benefit is plausible but not concretely isolated in results.

identified_claims.claim_label: MC datasets have weaknesses; SD17 remedies compositionality issue
identified_claims.claim_text: Available Morpho Challenge benchmark datasets contain weaknesses (non-compositional and trivial instances) that can mask the benefit of semantic-aware methods; the authors introduce a new semantically driven English dataset (SD17) addressing these weaknesses.
evidence: Authors enumerate issues in MC: non-compositional annotations (business), trivial instances (genitive, hyphenated), annotation inconsistencies, and bias towards affix- or lemma-completeness (Section 4.3).
SD17 created by sampling 2K words from top-10k frequency and annotating for compositional segmentation; inter-annotator agreement 91% and post-discussion 99% with removals (Section 4.3).
Results on SD17 show much larger MORSE advantage vs Morfessor (~24% absolute), which authors interpret as MC underestimating semantic methods' benefits (Section 5.2).
uncertainty_flags: SD17 sampling from top 10k frequency may bias dataset toward frequent/regular morphological patterns and away from low-frequency phenomena—authors note this but don't quantify effect.
Annotation protocol details, decision rules, and examples are summarized but full annotation guideline transparency or inter-annotator disagreement cases are not provided in manuscript.
Claim that SD17 'remedies' MC weaknesses is supported in part (addresses compositionality), but SD17 may introduce its own coverage biases.

identified_claims.claim_label: MORSE achieves SOTA improvements on English/Turkish but not Finnish
identified_claims.claim_text: MORSE achieves state-of-the-art or substantially improved intrinsic performance over Morfessor and other published results on English and Turkish (but not Finnish), with larger gains on the compositionality-aware dataset.
evidence: Table 3: MORSE F1 > Morfessor F1 on English (70.32 vs 64.35) and Turkish (38.07 vs 31.01), worse on Finnish (14.98 vs 34.06).
Text reports large gains on SD17 vs Morfessor (~24% absolute) and better than published LLSM (Narasimhan et al.) per Table 7 mention.
uncertainty_flags: Comparisons to 'published state-of-the-art' rely on reported numbers from prior work that may have used different preprocessing, vocabularies, or embeddings; direct reproducibility comparisons are limited.
No statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported, so magnitude claims ('substantially improved') are based on point estimates only.

Finnish failure is plausibly due to sparsity and 1M vocabulary cap, but quantification linking vocabulary cutoff to performance drop is not provided; thus the cross-lingual generality claim is partially supported but circumscribed by data-coverage constraints.

identified_claims.claim_label: Semantic modeling reduces over-segmentation of non-compositional words
identified_claims.claim_text: MORSE’s semantic modeling reduces over-segmentation on non-compositional words (e.g., 'freshman') compared to MDL-based systems.
evidence: Authors evaluated a curated list of 100 non-compositional-looking words; MORSE produced 7 false morphemes whereas Morfessor produced 43 (Section 5.3).
Motivating examples and algorithmic design (local cosine and offset-consistency checks) explicitly target this failure mode (Sections 1 & 3).
uncertainty_flags: Curated negative set is small (100 words) and selection procedure is not fully specified—results may not generalize.
No statistical test or confidence intervals provided for the 7 vs 43 counts; potential annotator bias or tuning influence not fully controlled.

Some non-compositional phenomena (idioms, historical semantic shift) may not be fully captured by embedding-based signals especially for rare words; claim is supported on evaluated set but generalization remains uncertain.

strengths.title: Clear operationalization of vocabulary-wide semantic validator
strengths.description: Defines and implements scorer_sem and scorew_sem that operationalize difference-vector consistency across support sets for candidate orthographic rules.
evidence: Section 3.1 formal definitions and equations for scorer_sem and scorew_sem.
Training/inference pipeline using these scores is detailed in Section 3.2.

strengths.title: Empirical evaluation across languages and a targeted dataset
strengths.description: Evaluations include English, Turkish, Finnish on MC benchmarks and a newly constructed compositionality-driven SD17, showing where semantic cues help.
evidence: Tables and text in Sections 4 and 5 presenting MC and SD17 results and cross-lingual discussion.
SD17 construction and annotation agreement reported in Section 4.3.

strengths.title: Addressing practical failure mode (over-segmentation)
strengths.description: Directly targets over-segmentation on semantically non-compositional words with analysis showing fewer false segments on a negative set.
evidence: Section 5.3 comparison: MORSE 7 vs Morfessor 43 false morphemes on curated non-compositional set.
Motivating examples in Introduction and Section 3.

strengths.title: Public release of code and datasets (SD17 and negative set)
strengths.description: Authors commit to releasing source code and datasets (canonical and noncanonical SD17, negative set) enabling reproducibility and follow-up work.
evidence: Section 4.1, 4.3 and footnotes with public URLs (though proxied) for code and datasets.

concerns.title: Asymmetric experimental constraints (vocabulary cap vs baseline)
concerns.description: MORSE imposes a 1M vocabulary limit for word embeddings for computational efficiency, while Morfessor is not similarly restricted, which could disadvantage MORSE on languages with large productive morphology (Finnish). This undermines claims of 'vocabulary-wide' signals and complicates cross-system comparisons.
evidence: Section 4.1 states MORSE limited to top 1M vocabulary; Section 5.1/Discussion ties Finnish underperformance to vocabulary cap.
Shared analysis explicitly highlights 'The effect of vocabulary truncation (1M limit) on availability of support pairs... can affect claims about 'vocabulary-wide' signals.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coverage statistics: for each dataset/language, provide counts/percentages of gold test words and support pairs present in the 1M vocabulary; run an ablation by increasing vocabulary (or sampling subset of Morfessor's input) to isolate vocabulary-cap effect.

concerns.title: Insufficient ablation isolating semantic components
concerns.description: The integrated pipeline uses orthographic counts, local cosine, and offset-consistency. The manuscript lacks controlled ablation experiments isolating the unique contributions of (a) local cosine only, (b) offset-consistency only, and (c) combined use, preventing clear attribution of performance gains.
evidence: Sections 3 and 5 describe combined scoring but provide no table comparing ablations.
Multiple reviewers in prior-stage digests pointed out lack of ablation isolating vocabulary-wide offset consistency vs local cosine vs orthographic support.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablation experiments (MORSE variants): orthography-only (baseline), orthography+local-cosine, orthography+offset-consistency, and full MORSE. Report boundary-F1 on MC and SD17 with statistical variance and discuss differential contributions.

concerns.title: Underspecified embedding training and hyperparameter reporting
concerns.description: Key embedding/training hyperparameters (CBOW vs skip-gram, epochs, min-count, negative sampling, random seed) and exact threshold values used for reported results are not fully enumerated. This hampers reproducibility and assessment of sensitivity to embedding quality.
evidence: Section 4.1 states Word2Vec 300d window=5 but omits CBOW/skip-gram, epochs, min-count, negative sampling, seed.
Prior-stage reviewers noted thresholds (cosine > 0.1) and other hyperparameters lack justification and full tabulation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a table listing all embedding training hyperparameters and the exact MORSE hyperparameters (tr_sem, tr_orth, tw_sem, tloc_sem) used per experiment. Include sensitivity plots (or at least ranges) showing robustness.

concerns.title: Asymmetric tuning and potential evaluation bias
concerns.description: MORSE requires small gold tuning data (authors state ~300 examples sufficient). The tuning/validation procedure for Morfessor and the other baselines is not fully described; asymmetric tuning could produce unfair comparisons.
evidence: Section 4.2 says MC training is used to tune MORSE hyperparameters; it's unclear whether Morfessor was tuned on same splits or default settings.
Prior-stage digests flagged 'asymmetric tuning and comparison procedure' as a top concern.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: State and apply the same tuning regimen to all methods or report results under multiple conditions (default Morfessor, Morfessor tuned on same dev set). Report performance variation under different tuning sizes for all systems where applicable.

concerns.title: Limited statistical reporting and small curated tests
concerns.description: Results are reported as point estimates without variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing; curated tests (100 negative examples) are small and selection process is underspecified.
evidence: Tables present single F1/precision/recall numbers; text mentions 5-fold CV for SD17 but no variances shown.
Non-compositional set size=100 and non-disclosure of selection criteria beyond examples.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report standard deviations/confidence intervals for cross-validation runs; apply statistical tests (e.g., paired bootstrap) when comparing systems. Provide full list and selection criteria of negative/curated tests in supplementary.

concerns.title: Greedy inference without global decoding
concerns.description: Inference greedily applies high-scoring add/replace rules iteratively; authors note cascading errors. No alternative (global or dynamic) decoding baseline is provided to quantify potential gains from non-greedy inference.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes greedy iterative inference; Section 6 admits greedy inference limits performance.
Related-stage reviewers noted greedy inference as potential failure mode without proposed alternatives.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a small-scale experiment comparing greedy inference to a beam search or dynamic programming/global optimization on a subset of data to quantify inference-induced errors.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary orthography-only baseline for unsupervised morpheme segmentation.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Morfessor uses MDL and orthographic cues; MORSE adds semantic validators (local cosine and offset-consistency).
comparable_works.source_trace: Related Work section cites Creutz and Lagus (2002, 2005, 2007) and comparisons in Sections 4-5.

comparable_works.relevance: Closest work using difference vectors for morphology induction; provides precedent for offset-based morphological modeling.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Soricut & Och used vector offsets to induce morphological transformations; MORSE adapts offset-consistency as a vocabulary-wide validator for orthographic rules. The manuscript cites Soricut & Och and claims to be first to use vocabulary-wide consistency specifically for morpheme segmentation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related Work mentions Soricut and Och (2015) and motivates MORSE's use of difference vectors.

comparable_works.relevance: Published semantic-aware morpheme segmentation approach used as a comparative baseline in the manuscript.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: LLSM uses semantic relatedness as part of a log-linear model; MORSE introduces vocabulary-wide offset consistency in addition to local semantic checks.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sections 1, 5 mention LLSM and compare reported numbers in Table 7 (text).

uncertainty_flags: Effect of the 1M vocabulary cap on support set availability and per-language coverage is not quantified; this materially affects 'vocabulary-wide' claim.
Hyperparameter choices (thresholds, embedding training details) are underspecified; results may be sensitive.
No ablation disentangles contribution of vocabulary-wide offset-consistency vs local cosine; causal attribution of gains remains uncertain.
Comparisons to published SOTA rely on reported numbers with possible preprocessing/experimental differences; direct comparability is uncertain without reimplementation.
Small size and selection of curated negative and SD17 sampling from top 10k frequency may bias results.
alternative_interpretations: Observed gains on English and Turkish may be driven primarily by filtering noisy orthographic pairs using local cosine similarity rather than by the novel vocabulary-wide offset measure; without ablation this remains plausible.

Large SD17 gains could partly reflect dataset sampling bias (top 10k frequent words and removal of ambiguous cases) that favors embedding-based methods over MDL methods; the difference may shrink on a more diverse frequency distribution.
Finnish underperformance might be attributable not only to vocabulary cap but also to intrinsic limitations of additive/concatenative rule enumeration for agglutinative/non-concatenative morphology.
transparency_notes: Provide full exact hyperparameter lists (embedding and MORSE thresholds), random seeds, preprocessing scripts, and stable repository URLs to enable reproducibility.
Release full SD17 annotation guidelines, raw annotations including disagreement cases, and the curated negative set with selection criteria.
Report per-language coverage: fraction of test words present in embedding vocab and fraction of support pairs found to make explicit data-availability constraints.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The idea of leveraging vector offsets has precedents (Soricut & Och), so the key novelty is operationalizing offset-consistency at the rule/support-set scale for morpheme segmentation rather than inventing a wholly new mechanism. Novelty is a signal but does not substitute for experimental isolation of the component's effect.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If embeddings are trained on sufficiently large corpora (covering bases and inflected forms), vocabulary-wide support sets will be dense and offset-consistency will robustly identify productive affix transformations, leading to gains across morphologically rich languages.
If hyperparameters (cosine cutoff, support size thresholds) are carefully tuned and validated with statistical rigor, the semantic validators will reduce over-segmentation without harming recall.

If inference is replaced with beam search or global decoding, cascading greedy errors will be reduced and combined semantic+orthographic signals will yield further improvements, particularly for multi-affix words.

novelty_lenses.rationale: MORSE composes existing ideas (orthographic rule enumeration, local cosine checks, and vector-offset regularities) into a practical pipeline with improvements on standard benchmarks; the primary novelty is the rule-level offset-consistency statistic and its use as a vocabulary-wide validator.
evidence: Related Work cites prior uses of semantic relatedness and offset-based morphology; Sections 3.1–3.2 show operationalization at rule/support-set scale.
uncertainty_flags: Unique contribution not isolated by ablation; similarity to Soricut & Och requires clearer differentiation.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The method does not introduce a fundamentally new modeling paradigm (still enumerative, greedy inference, concatenative rules) and relies on established embedding properties; gains are meaningful but bounded and contingent on embedding coverage and tuning.
evidence: Inference remains greedy and concatenative; authors mention future work needed for non-concatenative morphology and global inference.
Empirical improvements are dataset- and coverage-dependent (Finnish failure).
uncertainty_flags: If vocabulary and embedding constraints were lifted and ablations confirmed offset-consistency as principal driver, the disruptive claim would be stronger.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have medium-to-high confidence in the reported directionality of empirical findings (semantic signals help on English/Turkish and on compositionality-aware SD17; vocabulary cap harms performance in morphologically rich languages). However, uncertainties about hyperparameter tuning, asymmetric experimental setup, lack of ablation and statistical testing reduce confidence in magnitude/generalizability claims. The interval reflects this calibrated uncertainty.

consensus_findings: MORSE is a coherent, implementable system that augments orthographic candidate rule induction with two semantic validators: local pairwise cosine similarity and a vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency score (scorer_sem / score_w_sem).

On English and Turkish Morpho Challenge data MORSE shows improved boundary-level F1 relative to an orthography-only baseline (Morfessor) and shows substantially larger gains on the authors' SD17 compositionality-focused English dataset.
The vocabulary-wide difference-vector idea is a plausible and potentially useful incremental contribution (operationalized as rule-level scoring), building on prior uses of vector offsets in NLP.
MORSE reduces a targeted failure mode of orthography-only systems (over-segmentation of semantically non-compositional-looking words) on the small curated negative set used by the authors.

The method's effectiveness is conditional: it depends on embedding quality, vocabulary coverage (support sets), and hyperparameter choices; performance degrades on Finnish, plausibly due to data sparsity and the 1M vocabulary cap used in experiments.

Authors provide code and new dataset (SD17), increasing reproducibility potential, but several experimental/implementation details necessary to fully reproduce and evaluate claims are not exhaustively documented in the manuscript.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: reviewers differ in tone. Some characterize MORSE as a meaningful incremental engineering advance (operationalizing vocabulary-wide offsets at rule level); others urge caution about 'first' claims relative to Soricut & Och (2015) and related offset-based prior work. The disagreement centers on framing novelty (precise boundary vs. sweeping 'firstness').

Magnitude and attribution of empirical gains: reviewers agree gains exist for English/Turkish/SD17 but disagree about how much of the gain is due to the vocabulary-wide offset-consistency signal versus other factors (local cosine, orthographic frequency filtering, tuning regimen, dataset sampling). Some assess the evidence as sufficient; others find the causal attribution weak without ablations.

Severity of experimental asymmetries: reviewers unanimously flag experimental asymmetries (vocabulary cap, tuning procedures), but differ on whether these materially undermine the central empirical claims. Some see them as fixable caveats; others judge them as major methodological gaps that must be addressed to support the 'vocabulary-wide' claim.
uncertainty_hotspots: Vocabulary truncation to 1M tokens: how much does the cap reduce support-set coverage and thereby the utility of 'vocabulary-wide' consistency? No scaling experiments were reported. This is a principal uncertainty affecting cross-lingual generality (Finnish result) and the validity of the 'vocabulary-wide' descriptor.

Ablation of semantic components: absent controlled experiments isolating (a) orthography-only, (b) orthography + local cosine, (c) orthography + vocabulary-wide offsets, (d) full system. Without this, attribution of gains to the vocabulary-wide offset mechanism remains uncertain.

Hyperparameter choices and embedding training details: exact values (e.g., cosine threshold 0.1, tr_sem/tr_orth/tw_sem/tloc_sem), Word2Vec settings (CBOW/skipgram, epochs, min_count, negative sampling, seed) and their sensitivity are underreported. Results may be hyperparameter-sensitive.

Tuning and evaluation symmetry: MORSE requires small gold tuning data; it is unclear whether baselines (Morfessor and published systems) were tuned under symmetric regimens for the reported comparisons, particularly on SD17.

Dataset construction biases: SD17 samples from the top-10k frequency band and removed ambiguous items; this may favor embedding-based methods (better embeddings for frequent words). The degree to which SD17 generalizes to lower-frequency or typologically different phenomena is uncertain.
Greedy inference effects: greedy, iterative segmentation may cause cascading errors; no global/beam decoding baseline was presented to quantify potential losses from greedy choices.
model_diversity_effects: Semantic signals interact with orthographic heuristics in non-linear ways: vocabulary-wide offset-consistency tends to validate frequent, well-supported orthographic rules (amplifying precision) while local cosine can rescue some low-support but semantically tight pairs (balancing recall).

Embedding coverage and quality create role-specific effects: for languages and frequency bands where embeddings are high-quality (English, Turkish frequent forms), semantic components substantially improve segmentation; for low-coverage, morphologically productive languages (Finnish) semantic signals either provide little benefit or actively harm performance due to noisy/absent support pairs.

Tuning/data-regime dependence: requiring a small tuning set to set semantic thresholds means model diversity (different hyperparameter settings, embedding seeds) will influence which semantic signals dominate; asymmetric tuning across systems can produce apparent gains attributable to tuning regime rather than algorithmic superiority.

Computational constraints (vocab cap) bias the effective model: restricting to a top-N vocabulary concentrates support pairs among frequent word forms, which amplifies the influence of frequency-based orthographic patterns; this can make the 'vocabulary-wide' signal more a high-frequency signal than truly corpus-spanning.
meta_review.editor_guidance:
Key points for editorial attention (decision-making authority retained by editor):
- The submission offers a technically reasonable, reproducible-seeming pipeline and novel operationalization of vocabulary-wide offset consistency, and shows empirical gains on English and Turkish and on a new compositionality-focused dataset. These are substantive contributions of interest to the community.
- However, methodological gaps limit the conclusiveness of the central novelty and causal claims: missing ablations (to isolate vocabulary-wide offsets), lack of scaling experiments for the 1M vocabulary cap, underspecified embedding/hyperparameter reporting, and asymmetric tuning/comparison concerns. These affect generality claims across languages and the asserted 'vocabulary-wide' novelty.
- Recommended editorial paths (choose one or combine as fit policy):
  1) Invite a revision addressing core methodological gaps before publication: (a) ablation experiments separating semantic components, (b) vocabulary-size sensitivity experiments (or at minimum coverage statistics linking 1M cap to support-set loss), (c) full hyperparameter and embedding training specifications, and (d) symmetric tuning procedures for baselines. Also request statistical variance/CI reporting.
  2) If the venue accepts incremental method+dataset papers and can accommodate a 'strong revision required' decision, require the authors to at minimum add ablation and transparency artifacts in a reproducible supplement; accept conditional on reviewers confirming adequacy.
- Emphasize to authors that claims of being 'first' should be precisely worded and bounded, distinguishing operational instantiation from conceptual precedents (e.g., Soricut & Och).
meta_review.author_guidance:
Concrete, prioritized actions to improve the manuscript and strengthen claims:
1) Ablations: run and report controlled ablations with these variants: (A) orthography-only (scorer_orth), (B) orthography + local cosine only, (C) orthography + vocabulary-wide offset-consistency only, (D) full system. Provide boundary-level P/R/F1 for each language and SD17, with variance (cross-val folds or bootstrap CIs).
2) Vocabulary-cap sensitivity: quantify the impact of the 1M vocabulary cap. At minimum report (per language): fraction of test words in the MORSE embedding vocab, fraction of support pairs lost due to truncation, and an experiment varying vocab size (e.g., 100k, 500k, 1M, if resources permit) to show how scorer_sem and final performance scale.
3) Hyperparameters and embedding details: provide a full table of embedding training settings (CBOW/skipgram, epochs, min_count, negative samples, subsampling, learning rate, random seed) and all MORSE thresholds/values used per experiment. If possible, include sensitivity plots for the cosine threshold and the main hyperparameters.
4) Symmetric tuning of baselines: ensure Morfessor and other compared systems are tuned on the same development data or report both default and tuned baseline results. For SD17, include baseline results under the same 5-fold CV regime used for MORSE-CV.
5) Statistical reporting: add standard deviations/confidence intervals (e.g., bootstrap) for reported F1s and statistical tests where appropriate, and expand the curated negative set analysis (or at least provide full list and selection criteria) and compute significance for the 7 vs 43 counts.
6) Clarify novelty claims: revise wording around 'first' and explicitly contrast MORSE to Soricut & Och (2015) and Narasimhan et al. (2015), detailing algorithmic/operational differences and why the vocabulary-wide rule-level scorer differs from prior offset uses.
7) Inference ablation: provide at least a small-scale experiment comparing greedy inference with a non-greedy alternative (beam search or dynamic programming) to measure effect of cascading errors.
8) Dataset transparency: release full SD17 annotation guidelines, examples, eliminated/disagreed items, and basic statistics (frequency bins, POS distribution) and discuss how sampling choices may favor semantic methods; consider adding lower-frequency samples if feasible.
Implementing items 1-4 would materially reduce the main uncertainties raised by reviewers and substantively strengthen claims about the vocabulary-wide offset mechanism.
transparency_report: Provided: formal definitions and equations for scorer_sem, score_w_sem, score_loc_sem and the overall algorithmic pipeline (training + greedy inference), which aids reproducibility at a conceptual level.
Provided: code and dataset release claims (links in manuscript) including SD17 canonical/noncanonical and the negative set, improving practical reproducibility potential.

Missing / incomplete in manuscript: exact Word2Vec training hyperparameters (CBOW/skip-gram choice, epochs, min_count, negative sampling, subsampling, seeds), complete table of MORSE hyperparameter values used in each experiment, and precise tuning procedures applied to baselines (Morfessor) and published comparisons.

Missing / incomplete in manuscript: vocabulary coverage statistics showing how the 1M embedding cap affects test-word/support-pair availability, and absence of scaling experiments varying vocabulary size.

Missing / incomplete in manuscript: ablation results isolating the contributions of orthographic, local semantic, and vocabulary-wide semantic components; also missing variance estimates or statistical significance measures for reported P/R/F1 results.

Provided but needs extension: SD17 creation protocol summary and inter-annotator agreement; however the full annotation guidelines, eliminated disagreements, and dataset statistics should be released (or linked) for transparency.
epistemic_limits:
What cannot be resolved from the current manuscript and data provided:
- The unique causal contribution of the vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency component (scorer_sem) to the reported performance gains cannot be established without the requested ablation experiments; current results conflate multiple interacting signals and tuning effects.
- The extent to which the 1M vocabulary cap alters the practical meaning of 'vocabulary-wide' and its effect on morphologically rich languages (e.g., Finnish) remains unknown absent vocabulary-scaling experiments or per-word coverage statistics.
- Generalization to lower-frequency vocabulary strata and to typologically different morphologies (highly agglutinative or non-concatenative languages beyond the three evaluated) is uncertain, because SD17 samples from high-frequency English words and the Finnish failure was not isolatable to a single cause.
- The sensitivity of reported improvements to embedding training choices (algorithm, epochs, min_count) and to the cosine threshold (0.1) is not determined; results may change under different embedding regimes or seeds.
- Without symmetric tuning and replication of baselines under identical preprocessing and tuning regimens, comparative claims (including 'state-of-the-art') are provisional and contingent on reproducible re-execution under controlled settings.
These epistemic limits can be substantially reduced by the authors performing and reporting the ablation, vocabulary-scaling, hyperparameter disclosure/sensitivity analyses, and symmetric baseline tuning experiments recommended above.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces MORSE, an unsupervised morpheme-segmentation pipeline that augments orthographic candidate-rule induction with two semantic validators: (a) local pairwise relatedness (cosine similarity) and (b) a vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency score computed across support pairs. Experiments on Morpho Challenge English and Turkish show improved boundary-level F1 over an orthography-only baseline (Morfessor) and much larger gains on a newly released, compositionality-focused English dataset (SD17). The system underperforms on Finnish, which authors attribute to embedding sparsity and a 1M vocabulary cap. The idea of aggregating difference-vector consistency at the rule/support-set level is a plausible incremental contribution, but important methodological gaps (missing ablations, vocabulary-cap sensitivity, underspecified embedding/hyperparameter details, and asymmetric tuning of baselines) limit causal attribution and generality.
strengths: Clear operationalization of semantic validators: the paper gives explicit formulas for rule-level scorer_sem and pair-level score_w_sem and integrates them with orthographic support counts in a concrete pipeline.

Empirical breadth: experiments include multiple languages (English, Turkish, Finnish) and introduce SD17, a publicly released, compositionality-focused English dataset that highlights semantic-method advantages.

Practical failure-mode focus: the method targets over-segmentation of semantically non-compositional items and reports targeted reductions on a curated negative set; code and datasets are stated to be released, aiding reproducibility.
limitations: No controlled ablation isolating contributions of the three signal types (orthography-only; orthography + local cosine; orthography + vocabulary-wide offsets; full system). Without this, attribution of empirical gains to the vocabulary-wide offset mechanism remains uncertain.

Vocabulary coverage / scalability limitation: MORSE used a 1M-word embedding vocabulary cap for efficiency. The manuscript does not quantify how this truncation changes support-set availability or performance, undermining the 'vocabulary-wide' claim and leaving cross-lingual generality (e.g., Finnish) unresolved.

Underspecified embedding and hyperparameter details: key Word2Vec settings (CBOW vs skip-gram, epochs, min_count, negative sampling, seeds) and exact MORSE thresholds (tr_sem, tr_orth, tw_sem, tloc_sem and rationale for cosine > 0.1) are not fully tabulated, hindering reproducibility and obscuring sensitivity.

Asymmetric tuning/comparison concerns: MORSE requires tuning on gold examples; it is unclear whether baselines (Morfessor and reported published numbers) were tuned under equivalent regimes or evaluated under symmetric cross-validation conditions, raising possible evaluation bias.
open_questions: Can the authors provide ablation results for (a) orthography-only, (b) orthography + local cosine, (c) orthography + vocabulary-wide offset-consistency, and (d) the full MORSE pipeline, with boundary-level P/R/F1 and variance for each language and SD17?

How does performance (candidate rule counts, scorer_sem values, and final segmentation F1) vary with embedding vocabulary size? Please report coverage (% of test words in embedding vocab), and if feasible, an experiment varying vocab cutoff (e.g., 100k, 500k, 1M) to quantify the 1M cap effect.

Please list full embedding training hyperparameters (CBOW/skip-gram, epochs, min_count, negative sampling, subsampling, learning rate, random seed) and the exact MORSE hyperparameter values used in each experiment; additionally, provide sensitivity analyses for the cosine threshold (0.1) and other key thresholds.

Were baselines (Morfessor and other compared systems) tuned on the same development data or evaluated under symmetric cross-validation for SD17? If not, provide baseline results under matching tuning regimes (including Morfessor tuned via the same folds) to ensure fair comparison.
consensus_snapshot: MORSE is a coherent, implementable method that combines orthographic rule induction with local and corpus-level semantic validators, and the paper documents the algorithm and presents empirical gains on English and Turkish and strong gains on SD17.
Vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency, operationalized as rule-level scorer_sem, is a plausible incremental contribution building on prior offset/vector-arithmetic work.

The approach's effectiveness is conditional: it depends on embedding quality, vocabulary coverage, and hyperparameter settings; these boundary conditions are not fully characterized in the manuscript.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty framing: reviewers disagree on strength of the 'first' novelty claim. Some view MORSE's vocabulary-wide operationalization as a meaningful incremental innovation; others urge tempering strong 'firstness' claims given related prior work (e.g., Soricut & Och 2015).

Causal attribution of gains: reviewers differ on whether presented results sufficiently show that vocabulary-wide offsets (rather than local cosine, orthographic heuristics, or tuning choices) are the primary driver of improvement; some find the evidence convincing, others find it inconclusive without ablation.
Severity of experimental asymmetries: reviewers concur asymmetries exist (vocab cap, tuning), but differ on whether these are fatal to the central empirical claims or represent resolvable caveats.
uncertainty_snapshot: Degree to which the 1M vocabulary cap limited support-pair discovery and whether expanding vocab would recover Finnish performance.
Sensitivity of final segmentation performance to embedding training choices and to the chosen cosine threshold for offset consistency (0.1).
Whether SD17 sampling from frequent words and removal of ambiguous cases biases results toward embedding-based methods and inflates observed gains relative to more inclusive benchmarks.
Magnitude and statistical significance of reported improvements: point estimates are given but variance/confidence intervals and statistical tests are largely absent.
source_trace: Soricut, R. and Och, F. J. (2015). Work using vector offsets for morphological/lexical transformations; cited by authors as inspiration for difference-vector usage (Related Work in manuscript).
Mikolov, T. et al. (2013). Word2Vec and vector arithmetic motivation (authors cite Mikolov et al. for offset intuition; embedding training used in experiments).
Creutz & Lagus (Morfessor). Morfessor is used as primary orthography/MDL baseline in experiments and is discussed in Related Work and Results (Sections 2, 4, 5 of manuscript).
Narasimhan et al. (2015) (LLSM). Prior semantic-aware segmentation approach referenced and compared in results; relates to local cosine-based methods referenced in manuscript.
Morpho Challenge datasets. Commonly used benchmarks (English, Turkish, Finnish) used in paper's evaluations; manuscript argues these contain non-compositional/trivial instances (Section 4.3).
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides formal definitions for the semantic and orthographic scores and outlines the training/inference pipeline; code and datasets (SD17 and negative set) are stated to be released. However, key experimental details required for exact reproduction are missing or incomplete in the manuscript: full Word2Vec training hyperparameters (CBOW/skip-gram, epochs, min_count, negative samples, subsampling, seeds), precise MORSE hyperparameter values and thresholds used per experiment, coverage statistics showing how the 1M embedding vocabulary affects test-word/support-pair availability, and explicit documentation of baseline tuning procedures. The SD17 annotation protocol and eliminated/disagreement cases should be included/released to improve dataset transparency.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The submission presents a technically coherent method and useful dataset with empirical gains of interest, but several methodological gaps constrain the strength of its claims. Recommended editorial actions: request a revision that addresses core reproducibility and attribution concerns before acceptance. At minimum, require (1) controlled ablation experiments isolating orthography-only, orthography+local-cosine, orthography+offset-consistency, and full MORSE, (2) explicit embedding and MORSE hyperparameter tables and sensitivity analyses (including justification/sweeps for cosine threshold), (3) vocabulary-coverage statistics and, if feasible, limited experiments varying vocabulary cutoff to show sensitivity, and (4) symmetric tuning of baselines (e.g., Morfessor) or reporting baseline results under matching tuning regimes. Also ask authors to temper 'first' novelty phrasing and to release full code, exact configuration files, SD17 annotation guidelines, and eliminated/disagreement lists.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Prioritized actions to strengthen the paper: 1) Add ablation experiments comparing orthography-only, orthography + local cosine, orthography + vocabulary-wide offsets, and full MORSE with boundary P/R/F1 and variance for each dataset/language. 2) Provide full embedding training settings (CBOW/skip-gram, epochs, min_count, negative samples, subsampling, learning rate, random seeds) and a table of MORSE hyperparameters (values tried and chosen). 3) Quantify the impact of the 1M vocabulary cap: report percent coverage of test words and support pairs, and run limited experiments varying vocab cutoff if resources permit. 4) Ensure baselines are tuned symmetrically (or report both default and tuned baseline numbers), especially for SD17 where MORSE used cross-validation. 5) Add statistical reporting (confidence intervals or bootstrap tests) for F1 differences and expand the negative-set analysis (release the list and selection criteria). 6) Clarify novelty statements by precisely contrasting MORSE with closest prior work (Soricut & Och 2015; Narasimhan et al. 2015). 7) If possible, include a small experiment comparing greedy inference to a non-greedy alternative (beam search or DP) to measure cascading error effects. Addressing items 1-4 will materially reduce reviewers' main uncertainties.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The manuscript proposes MORSE, which augments orthographic morpheme-rule induction with two semantic validators: local cosine similarity and a vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency metric. Results show improved boundary-F1 on English and Turkish and large gains on a new compositionality-focused English dataset (SD17); performance drops on Finnish, attributed to sparsity and a 1M embedding vocabulary cap.

Strengths: MORSE operationalizes corpus-level offset consistency with explicit formulas (scorer_sem, score_w_sem), integrates semantic and orthographic cues into a reproducible-seeming pipeline, evaluates across languages and on a new dataset (SD17), targets a practical failure mode (over-segmentation), and releases code/datasets.

Limitations: 1) No ablation isolating the unique contributions of vocabulary-wide offsets vs local cosine vs orthography; causal attribution is therefore uncertain. 2) The 1M-word vocabulary cap is an implementation constraint that is not analyzed quantitatively; it may materially affect the 'vocabulary-wide' claim and explain cross-lingual failures (Finnish). 3) Embedding training and MORSE hyperparameters (including the cosine > 0.1 cutoff) are underreported, impairing reproducibility and sensitivity assessment. 4) Tuning/evaluation asymmetry (MORSE tuned on gold examples; baseline tuning unclear) could bias comparative claims, especially on SD17.

Open Questions: 1) Please provide ablation results for the four system variants (orthography-only; orthography + local cosine; orthography + offsets; full). 2) How does performance scale with embedding vocabulary size? Provide coverage stats and (if possible) a limited vocab-size sweep. 3) List complete embedding hyperparameters and MORSE thresholds; show sensitivity to the cosine threshold. 4) Were baselines tuned under identical procedures (especially for SD17)? If not, provide baseline results under symmetric tuning.

Transparency: The paper includes formal algorithmic definitions and states code/dataset release, which is positive. To reach reproducibility standards, the repository should include exact configuration files, Word2Vec training scripts and seeds, parameter grids, SD17 annotation guidelines and disagreement cases, preprocessing scripts, and instructions to reproduce reported tables. Statistical variance (CIs, bootstrap) should be added to reported metrics.

confidence_interval.rationale: There is moderate-to-high confidence in the paper's core engineering and that reported empirical gains (English/Turkish and SD17) exist under the described settings. However, uncertainties about ablation (causal attribution), vocabulary-cap effects, embedding/hyperparameter sensitivity, and asymmetric tuning of baselines materially affect confidence in the magnitude, generality, and novelty framing of claims; addressing the recommended experiments would raise confidence.
